prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks satisfy the test I take from the prize criteria, a specific discovery or invention rather than a body of work. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift while holding many atoms without Doppler or recoil broadening, and this is a single idea whose performance is measured rather than inferred. Four of us ranked it first and the two remaining rankings are 5 and 7, so there is breadth here that no other entry matches. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: every one of the six members who ranked it proposed the same two names, Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the clocks to record stability and accuracy. The achievement is mature, reproduced and surpassed in many laboratories, and it is the working basis for the coming redefinition of the second, for tests of fundamental constants and for relativistic geodesy.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that lattice clocks sit on already recognised foundations, namely laser cooling, the frequency comb (2005) and ion trapping and control (2012), so a sceptic can call this an outstanding refinement of precision metrology rather than a new discovery. The credit also leaves out ion-clock pioneers and other lattice-clock groups, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, which could argue for waiting. I judge these real but not decisive, since the lattice idea is a distinct invention with its own performance record.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B018 fifth and worries that earlier recognition of the frequency comb and ion-clock work may weigh against another precision-metrology prize, and that the pending redefinition of the second is a reason to wait.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but the comb is a tool in the clock and not the achievement, and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, not the neutral-atom lattice with its many-atom stability. Waiting for the redefinition of the second would tie a scientific prize to a metrological administrative decision; the discovery is already established by independent comparisons at 10^-18. I do agree that the citation must name the lattice clock specifically and not precision timekeeping in general, and I have written it that way. I also note that your own first choice, IceCube, is a strong alternative and I would not object to it as a later prize.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B018 seventh, accepting its importance but pointing to Hall and Hansch (2005) as overlap, and ranked Cirac and Zoller first as the theoretical blueprint behind a field of quantum control.
responses.response: I respect the Cirac-Zoller case on originality, but it is a theory-only prize for a field whose experimental half was recognised in 2012, and Lindroth's and your own notes on that point seem to me correct. For B018 the comb overlap is the lesser concern, because Katori's idea was a concept about trapping, not about frequency measurement. I also want to say plainly that your declared proximity to circuit QED means I discount your ranking of B008 in either direction, while your assessment of B018 as a clear two-person configuration supports my view.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B018 first but asks whether the committee would prefer to credit the broader optical-clock lineage, including ion clocks, rather than the lattice-clock step alone.
responses.response: I would keep the narrower citation. Widening it to the optical-clock lineage would drag in Hall, Hansch, Wineland-type ion clocks and Lemonde, which dilutes the attribution and conflicts with the criterion that the prize identify the topic and the people responsible for the original work. The lattice clock is the identifiable step, and two names is a defensible representation of it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked tunnel magnetoresistance (B003) second and values it as a natural successor to the GMR prize with enormous technological reach.
responses.response: I agree with the science of B003, and it was my own second choice for reasons of interface and barrier quality that I know from microscopy. My hesitation is attribution: the decisive coherent-tunnelling MgO step involves Yuasa, Djayaprawira and the Butler and Mathon theory, none of whom are in the credit, and Miyazaki and Moodera is a cleaner pair than the three-name credit suggests. Until that is sorted out I put it behind the lattice clock.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the earlier frequency-comb and ion-control prizes.
The boundary of credit relative to ion-clock pioneers and other lattice-clock groups is from my own recollection and not verified.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect timing, which I think it should not.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. A general connection to flag is my long-running academic exchange with Japanese universities, including a University of Tokyo fellowship, and Katori is based in Japan; this is institutional proximity, not a documented collaboration, and I do not think it requires recusal. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is a committee member but has no apparent link to this entry.
